subject: Critical Thinking
title: Hindsight Bias: I Knew It All Along
description: A short lesson to help you apply Hindsight Bias: I Knew It All Along.

hook.text: After every stock market crash, experts say 'the signs were obvious.' They never say it before the crash.

buildup.text: Hindsight bias: once we know an outcome, we believe we would have predicted it. We rewrite our own memory.

discovery.text: Fischhoff showed that people given outcomes rated them as 'obvious' – even when they couldn't predict them beforehand.

twist.text: This bias makes us overconfident about future predictions and unfairly harsh on people who 'should have known.'

climax.text: Hindsight bias corrupts learning — if you think you 'knew it all along,' you won't study what went wrong.

punchline.text: Everything is obvious after it happens.

quiz.question: What does hindsight bias cause people to believe?
options: That they would have predicted an outcome they already know

details.summary: Hindsight bias makes past events seem predictable after they happen. Once you know the outcome, your brain rewrites history to make it feel inevitable, destroying your ability to learn from surprises.
details.whyItMatters: Hindsight bias prevents learning from mistakes because you convince yourself you saw it coming. This makes future predictions overconfident.
takeaways: Outcomes feel inevitable only after they happen
Hindsight bias corrupts memory of your original predictions
Decision journals can counteract the effect

faq.question: How does hindsight bias affect learning from past decisions?
faq.answer: When you believe you predicted an outcome all along, you do not examine what you actually thought beforehand. This prevents honest analysis of your decision process and blocks genuine improvement.

faq.question: How can keeping a decision journal reduce hindsight bias?
faq.answer: Writing down your predictions and reasoning before outcomes are known creates an honest record. Reviewing these entries later reveals the gap between what you predicted and what you now remember predicting.
